images.caption: Photograph of Afghan chiefs and a British Political Officer posed at Jamrud fort at the mouth of the Khyber Pass, taken by John Burke in 1878. Burke, the most intrepid of the photographers active in Victorian India, accompanied nearly all of the British military campaigns of this period, but is best known for his photography during the Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878-80). He accompanied the Peshawar Valley Field Force during the two-year campaign and worked steadily in the hostile environment of Afghanistan and the North West Frontier Province (Pakistan), the scene of the military operations.

images.filename: Photograph of Jamrud Fort, taken by Dhanna Singh Chahal 'Patialvi', 1932.jpg
images.caption:
Photograph of Jamrud Fort, taken by Dhanna Singh Chahal 'Patialvi', 1932.
Image source URL: [1]
This photograph was showcased in a webinar titled 'De-Freezing 1930's Panjab', delivered on 20 August 2011, refer to: [2]; [3]; [4]; [5]


The image that we see on the screen is also deeply connected to the history of Punjab. Whenever it is even briefly mentioned, we begin to speak of a very long history. When something extremely difficult or seemingly impossible is done, an idiom is used—like the Fort of Jamrud. This fort was actually built in the 18th century by Hari Singh Nalwa. In 1837, Hari Singh Nalwa was martyred at this very fort. From the time it was built until today, this fort has remained extremely important for the entire region.
In history, we repeatedly see that invaders would enter through the Khyber Pass and attack Hindustan, causing destruction throughout the region. This fort continued to be significant even after the end of Ranjit Singh’s rule, then under the British, and later for Pakistan as well. Today it lies in Pakistan’s former Federally Administered Tribal Area, near Peshawar. Even now, it is under the control of the Pakistan Army. For the past 60 years, since the formation of Pakistan, this fort has remained under military control, and no kind of tourist activity has been allowed there.

When we look at this photograph, it leads our attention back to the person who took it—Bhai Dhanna Singh—and to his other photographs as well. Bhai Dhanna Singh belonged to the Patiala princely state. After visiting several gurdwaras in villages, he felt that it was necessary to preserve these gurdwaras through photography. For this purpose, he came to Patiala specifically to receive training in camera photography. The photograph of this fort was taken on 24 April 1932. Apart from this, there are no other known photographs of this fort from that time for historians or travelers.
